author: high
claim: The rank-pair plan directly proves the full monotone-subsequence theorem; status: solved.
evidence: Write the sequence as x_1,...,x_{n^2+1}. For each i, define a_i and b_i as the respective maximum lengths of increasing and decreasing subsequences ending at x_i; these maxima exist because the one-term subsequence is admissible and only finitely many subsequences end at i. If some a_i>=n+1 or b_i>=n+1, the required subsequence exists (and if its length exceeds n+1, taking its first n+1 terms gives exactly the requested length). Otherwise 1<=a_i,b_i<=n for every i. For i<j, either x_i<x_j, which gives a_j>=a_i+1 by appending x_j, or x_i>x_j, which gives b_j>=b_i+1. Thus all (a_i,b_i) are distinct. But the set {1,...,n}x{1,...,n} contains exactly n^2 ordered pairs, so it cannot contain the n^2+1 distinct pairs indexed by i. This contradiction finishes the proof.

links.subgoal: Prove the full theorem by injectivity of endpoint rank pairs and a finite counting contradiction.
links.attempt_summary: Both injectivity and counting subgoals are solved self-containedly.

glossary.n: the positive integer in the theorem
glossary.x_i: the real number in position i of the sequence
glossary.a_i: the maximum length of a strictly increasing subsequence ending at position i
glossary.b_i: the maximum length of a strictly decreasing subsequence ending at position i
